Chapel Royal. The collective name for the royal chapel institutions of the English monarchy, most prominently at the palaces of Westminster and St. James's. Functioning as the monarch's private chapel and a center of music performance, the Chapel Royal employed composers and singers who wrote and performed sacred music for the royal household. From the Tudor period through the eighteenth century, the Chapel Royal was one of Europe's most prestigious musical institutions, where master composers including Tallis, Byrd, and Purcell created some of England's greatest sacred music.

The Chapel Royal's tradition dates to medieval times but flourished particularly during the Tudor and Stuart periods of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, when the monarchy was politically stable and culturally ambitious. Thomas Tallis served the Chapel Royal for over forty years, spanning the reigns of Henry the Eighth through Elizabeth the First, composing anthems, motets, and masses that remain canonical to English church music.

Henry Purcell was one of the Chapel Royal's greatest composers, serving as organist and composer. His sacred music, anthems and services, combined English tradition with Continental Baroque sophistication. The Chapel Royal's master of the children directed the choir boys and oversaw their musical training. This position was often held by composers themselves, making it a coveted post combining performance, composition, and pedagogy.

The chapel maintained both a choir of singers and an ensemble of instrumentalists including viols, violins, and harpsichord, allowing composers to write polyphonic works of sophisticated textures and orchestration. George Frideric Handel served as Composer of the Chapel Royal near the end of his life, though the institution's musical prestige had begun to decline by the eighteenth century as secular concert life grew. The Chapel Royal's model influenced cathedral music throughout England and British Commonwealth nations. Many English cathedrals maintain choirs and musical traditions descended from Chapel Royal practices. The Chapel Royal connects to Henry Purcell, Thomas Tallis, George Frideric Handel, England, sacred music, Baroque music, and the anthem as its characteristic vocal form.
